Traupman 350

prope

adverb, and preposition with the accusative; comparative propius, superlative proximē

near, close by

As a preposition, with the accusative (prope urbem) or with ab (prope ā meīs aedibus, Cic. Pis. 26). Prope also means “almost” (see almost).

Other words

  • propinquus, propinqua, propinquum — near, nearby, neighbouring

    also used · classical · Cic. Rosc. Am. 133: propinquum praedium (Lewis & Short); Traupman 350 · Declension on Wiktionary

    The adjective; as a noun, a relative (propinquī, one’s relations).

  • proximus, proxima, proximum — nearest, next

    also used · classical · Cic. Att. 2.14.2: proximus est vīcīnus · Declension on Wiktionary

    The superlative: in proximō, nearby (Traupman 350).

  • vīcīnus, vīcīna, vīcīnum — neighbouring, near

    also used · classical · Hor. Ep. 1.14.24 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 350; Traupman 205 · Declension on Wiktionary

    As an adjective mostly poetic (Lewis & Short); as a noun, a neighbour (see neighbour).

  • juxtā — close by, right next to

    adverb, and preposition with the accusative · also used · classical · Caes. B.G. 2.26.1: legiō, quae juxtā cōnstiterat (Lewis & Short)

Examples

  • cēna brevis juvat et prope rīvum somnus in herbā

    I like a light dinner, and a nap in the grass near a streamHor. Ep. 1.14.35

  • cujus etiam illī hortulī propinquī nōn memoriam sōlum mihi adferunt, sed ipsum videntur in cōnspectū meō pōnere

    even his little gardens nearby not only bring him to mind but seem to set the man himself before my eyesCic. Fin. 5.2

  • in proximō

    nearbyTraupman 350

See also far, approach, neighbour, almost, local.
